item.content:encoded:
Hiring out definitely works better, yes!

Any other phrasings that stick out to you as particularly egregious?

Well, uh… ha! Now that you mention it…

World War I

This document is from 1932, so, in the words of David Mitchell, it would be the act of an "incredible pessimist" to call the Great War "World War One"… xD

I can try to do a comb-over of this at some point tonight if you'd like, but it's not just the lexicographical issues. It's the tone and presentation — it doesn't sound like something I'd expect a criminal to produce. Where's the alternate spellings? The street grammar? What form did this document exist in — why does it include photographs? Did this person actually go through the trouble of taking photographs in 1932, then label them, and insert them into this note for others to see? Etc.

Sorry if this is coming off as a bit harsh. A document like this is a huge challenge; I appreciate that you just went for it, but I also don't think this really 'recreates' the historical period to which it's supposed to belong.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
We started outsourcing.

There's several issues I have with this piece; this line's just one of them. What you're trying to do is really hard, so I can't fault you for trying (if anything, I like the fact that you just went for it like this; that's one reason I'm not down-voting).

On the other hand, a Chicago gang-member using a term like "outsourcing"? In 1931? This is what makes a document like this so challenging: You need to make it both historically sensible (it needs to look like something a 1931 anomalous criminal organization would produce) while also being compelling on its own.

This is a huge challenge, and something I would expect requires a lot of research to get "right". As an example of something I think does this just right: A History of Reaction, by TyGently.

item.content:encoded: I'm not too certain that the Spirit would have a "How We Made It" section in their formats. I would expect the format to be more utilitarian - only explaining what it is, when and how to use it, and how not to kill yourself in the process. I'm willing to excuse the Note from the Desk of Richard Chappell, but the rest is too exposition-heavy for my liking.

FWIW I wanted to give C-Spirit formats more of a narrative feel, since SCP-2680 and others rely on that sort of writing and my previous SCP-3855 was a bit too tonally detached compared to other Spirit skips.
